pieces.s: Five Canadian frauds, put back through the forensic screen ex ante
pieces.blurb: Five Canadian accounting frauds with completed regulatory or judicial findings — Sino-Forest, Nortel, Poseidon Concepts, Livent, Philip Services — put back through the Beneish M-Score on the filings that existed before each collapse. Zero of three computable test years flag at the standard cut-off, and the piece types every miss by its cause: threshold, mechanism, model scope, or archive failure. Every figure carries a provenance label, and the computation ships with the page.
pieces.demo: An interactive bench rebuilds each score from the filed figures and lets the reader drag the cut-off to watch sensitivity buy false positives.

pieces.s: Adversarial claim auditing: decompose, attack, grade what survives
pieces.blurb: A system that refuses to answer questions directly: it decomposes each one into individually falsifiable claims, files a falsifier and an evidence tier with every claim, and sets attack agents against them on provenance, inference, selection, and anachronism. The answer is whatever the surviving claims can carry, at the tier of the weakest load-bearing link. Three runs are on the record — a hindsight-locked backtest and two live audits — with graveyards, rejected attacks, and unabridged transcripts.
pieces.demo: The backtest run replays a question whose answer is now known with evidence locked at the cutoff, and returns UNDETERMINED: the leak test the live runs stand on.

pieces.t: Crucible Run 0: the Bank of Canada backtest
pieces.s: Evidence locked at January 2023; the engine says what was knowable
pieces.blurb: A BACKTEST-mode audit of a January 2023 rate-path question — will the Bank of Canada cut below 4.00% before July 31, 2024 — with every source barred after the cutoff date. Sixteen claims filed, one killed, and a reader verdict of UNDETERMINED at 0.50: the record available that day did not decide the question, and the engine says so rather than borrowing hindsight.

pieces.t: Crucible Run B: the maturity-wall thesis
pieces.s: The 2026 coupon step-up claim, audited and refuted
pieces.blurb: A LIVE-mode audit of the widely-circulated 2026 maturity-wall thesis for Canadian investment-grade issuers: that refinancing retired debt now costs more than 150 basis points of coupon. Forty-eight claims filed, four killed, and every construction of the issuer-level median step-up the retrievable record supports lands between +83 and +143 basis points — bounded, repeatedly, on the wrong side of the threshold. Direction: refuted, at 0.20.

pieces.t: Crucible Run C: the goodwill-impairment thesis
pieces.s: The too-little-too-late critique, audited against TSX issuers
pieces.blurb: A LIVE-mode audit of the claim that impairment-only goodwill accounting recognises losses too little and too late, tested against S&P/TSX Composite non-financial issuers that first recognised an impairment between 2022 and 2025. Forty-eight claims filed, seven killed, the halt reached on zero verdict changes, and a reader verdict of refuted at 0.30 on the claim as filed.

pieces.s: A pre-registered protocol on the Late Bronze Age collapse
pieces.blurb: A research protocol — methodology only, no results — for testing whether the Eastern Mediterranean collapsed around 1177 BCE because exogenous shocks struck a trade network optimised past the point of resilience, with the Sea Peoples as symptom rather than cause. Hypotheses, falsification conditions, data architecture, and the analysis plan are declared before any data is touched, and the abstract to be published if the central hypothesis fails is drafted in advance.
pieces.demo: Colour is used as a register throughout: each evidence stream — metals, network, textual, failure — carries its own colour, and nothing else does.

pieces.s: A pre-registered protocol on ESG-rating disagreement and portfolios
pieces.blurb: A research protocol — methodology only, no results — applying the same pre-registered discipline to ESG-rating divergence: what it costs a portfolio when the raters disagree about what the same company is. The measurement model, the errors-in-variables consequence for reported ESG alpha, the portfolio programs, the placebo the study lives or dies by, and the full robustness battery are declared in advance, with calibration tables and the statistical power computed before any test is run.

pieces.s: Sixty-two revenue scenarios, every answer anchored to the Handbook
pieces.blurb: A drill on revenue recognition under IFRS 15: 29 determinate items scored against the standard and 33 judgment items that show their reasoning, every answer carrying its paragraph or illustrative example, verified against Part I of the CPA Canada Handbook, 2026 Edition. Each item names the trap beside the treatment, because the wrong answer you almost gave is the thing worth studying.
pieces.demo: The bank distinguishes what the standard settles from what it leaves to judgment, and scores only the former: a trainer that scores nothing teaches nothing, and one that scores judgment calls teaches something false.

pieces.t: IFRS 15 Item Bank: Verification and Backfill
pieces.s: The verification memo behind the trainer
pieces.blurb: What was actually read to build the trainer: the full standard and all 65 illustrative examples in Part I of the CPA Canada Handbook, the four IFRIC agenda decisions read in full against the four left as leads, what the CSA staff notices really say, and the gaps recorded as gaps. Two verification passes are documented, including the correction each one forced.

pieces.s: Materiality and sampling under the CAS, requirements separated from habit
pieces.blurb: A research pack on materiality and audit sampling under the Canadian Auditing Standards, built around the small set of paragraphs that actually say shall. The five-per-cent-of-income benchmark, the performance materiality haircut and the clearly-trivial threshold are traced to where they really come from, which is firm methodology and habit rather than the standards themselves.

pieces.s: A 2022 documentary, claim by claim, against the 2026 record
pieces.blurb: CNN's Inside the Mind of Vladimir Putin, audited claim by claim four years on: four claims hold, four are overstated or unverified, one is factually wrong, and nine were overtaken by events. The history survives; every present tense in the film has expired, and the audit separates the three questions that is-this-still-valid bundles together.

pieces.s: The map, and the method that audits it
pieces.blurb: Fifteen systems and 148 couplings, annotated by an audit instrument that was run against its own falsification test and failed it. Every one of eighty claims carries the verdict three independent raters gave it, blind to the author, and a mark for whether its evidence can be retrieved at all.
pieces.demo: The instrument reports the result that undermines its own headline: panel-to-author agreement is 78 per cent, which is 22 per cent divergence against a 20 per cent withdrawal threshold the project set for itself before it knew the answer. The finding is published in its narrow form rather than its strong one, and 4 of 9 adversarial mutations are documented as still uncaught.

pieces.t: Predictive History: the withdrawn first edition
pieces.s: Kept uncorrected, with the divergence computed rather than described
pieces.blurb: The first edition, frozen at the point its numbers were withdrawn. Its banner computes the gap to the current panel rather than characterising it: dates read 100 per cent here against the panel's 60, the institutional row is missing entirely, and three further divergences are named row by row.
pieces.demo: A project about the distance between confident presentation and the record, showing its own. Nothing below the banner is corrected, and both columns of the comparison are computed at build time, the left by parsing this frozen file and the right from the current ledger.

pieces.s: A study edition of the AI capital-cycle adjudication
pieces.blurb: Seventeen figures built from the analysis's own numbers, under one rule: the fork between the two anchors is never closed, and any mark that arithmetic produced rather than an instrument measured is drawn open.
pieces.demo: The largest essay here (Crucible Run B is the largest piece on the site), and the one that shows the method at full size. Two rival readings of the same capital cycle are carried side by side to the end rather than averaged into one, and the page corrects its own arithmetic in public where a later attribution changed the base.

pieces.s: Corporate ethics and the micro/macro foundations of strategy
pieces.blurb: Eight questions, one repeating structure, and one recurring decision: where the accounting boundary sits, and whose losses fall outside it.
pieces.demo: An accounting question asked as an ethics question. Colour means one thing on every figure: blue is inside the accounting boundary and priced, red is outside it. A result that is not distinguishable from zero is drawn as an open outline at full size rather than shrunk to nothing.

pieces.s: An essay on the accounting of harm
pieces.blurb: When a firm harms someone who does not trade with it, the share price moves 0.24 per cent. Not significant. An essay on standing, externality, and who decides which losses count.
pieces.demo: The whole essay turns on a negative result, and reports it as one. Solid marks are quantities that reach someone's books; open outlines at full size are quantities that are real and appear on no invoice.

pieces.blurb: A fixed-unit data essay: one square is one trillion US dollars, declared once and never rescaled, with every figure carrying the provenance tag it was published under.
pieces.demo: A unit declared once and held for the whole document, so quantities stay comparable by eye across every figure. Two sources that disagree are shown side by side instead of averaged.
